---
title: "Concepts"
---

tether borrows its shape from [jj](https://jj-vcs.dev): there is a working copy
that gets snapshotted on every command, commits that record it, and `new` to
start working on top of a commit. What differs is *what* is versioned: not
files in a tree, but the state of external systems that keep their own
history.

## The working copy is the manifests

A dataset is a directory holding `tether.toml` and `.tether/objects/<key>.toml`,
one manifest per registered object. A manifest names the object (`kind` +
`locator`), its policy, and -- once committed -- its recorded `state` and, if
any, its `pin`. Committing a dataset means committing those manifests to the
enclosing git/jj repository. History, undo, bookmarks, workspaces, and sharing
are therefore the VCS's, not tether's.

| jj | tether |
| --- | --- |
| working copy | the VCS working dir; the committed thing is the manifests |
| snapshot on every command | **snapshot**: concurrent fan-out fingerprint of every object |
| `jj commit` | **pin** fan-out + write state into manifests + `jj/git commit` |
| `jj new <rev>` | checkout + **fork** fan-out (fresh writable branch per object) |
| stale working copy | manifest hash recorded at fork differs from HEAD: refuse writes |
| `jj diff` | **diff**: object-level manifest diff; `--content` asks each backend for its native diff |
| `jj log` | **log**: an object's *native* history (snapshots / versions / commits); ids feed `add --at` |
| detached head | an object registered `--at` a state that is not a branch head; `commit` pins it, `new` forks from it |
| -- | **verify** (pins still resolve) and **gc** (drop unreferenced pins, dead workspaces' branches) |
| `jj abandon` / `jj squash` | the VCS's own; what history no longer names, `gc` releases |

## State, pin, fork

For each object a backend implements three things, in increasing order of what
the system must support:

- **State**: what the object *is* right now -- an Icechunk `snapshot_id`, a
  Neon `(lsn, next_xid)`, a Delta `version`, a directory's size/mtime digest.
  Comparing states is how drift is detected without watching anything.
- **Pin**: a durable, GC-proof native reference to a state, named
  `tether.<pin_id>` -- an Icechunk tag, a protected Neon child branch, a git
  tag, a Lance tag, a Dolt tag. `pin_id = blake2b(kind, locator identity,
  state)[:12]`, so identical state on the same object yields the same pin and
  re-committing an unchanged object is a no-op.
- **Fork**: a fresh writable branch created off a pin -- or, for objects with
  `pin = "record"`, straight off the recorded state, skipping the native ref
  entirely. `tether new` forks one per Forkable object, named
  `tether.ws.<workspace-id>.<key>`, so workspaces never collide.

## Plans

Every command that writes to an external system (`commit` pins, `new` forks,
`gc` unpins and deletes branches) is a read-only **plan** followed by an
**apply**. `--dry-run` prints the plan, `--plan FILE` saves it, `--from-plan
FILE` applies it later; apply re-checks that states and manifests still match
what the plan recorded and refuses otherwise (`StalePlanError`). The Python API
exposes the same pairs: `plan_commit`/`apply_commit`, `plan_new`/`apply_new`,
`plan_gc`/`apply_gc`.

## Capability tiers

Backends declare capabilities; commands degrade explicitly by tier.

- **Observed** (`FINGERPRINT`): drift detection only. `commit` records the state
  and marks it `recoverable = false`. A local directory by mtime, an
  unversioned S3 prefix.
- **Addressable** (`+ ADDRESSABLE`): the recorded state can be read back later
  with nothing to create or GC. An S3 object in a versioned bucket, a Delta
  version, a DuckLake snapshot.
- **Pinnable** (`+ PIN`): a durable native ref can be created and deleted;
  `verify` and `gc` apply.
- **Forkable** (`+ FORK`): a writable branch can be created off a pin; `new`
  forks and `open` returns a writable handle. Icechunk, Neon, Iceberg, Lance,
  lakeFS, Dolt, git/jj.

Orthogonal flags refine behavior: `CHEAP_FINGERPRINT` (metadata only),
`RETENTION_BOUND` (recoverability expires with a retention window),
`NEEDS_QUIESCENCE` (commit checks for active writers), `ATOMIC_REF`
(create-if-absent pins), `DIFF` (native content diffs), `HISTORY` (native
log), `BRANCH_IS_STORAGE` (deleting a branch reclaims its data; `gc` never
prunes such a branch without force).

## Handles, not data

tether is never in the data path. `open` returns a typed handle carrying the
native address -- an Icechunk session on the right branch or tag, a Postgres
URL, a `DeltaTable` at a version, a `lakefs://repo/ref/prefix/` URI -- and steps
aside. You read and write with the system's own library.

## Stale working copies

`tether new` records the manifest hash it forked from. If HEAD's manifests
later change (someone committed, you switched revisions), the workspace is
*stale*: `status` says so and writable `open` refuses with
`StaleWorkingCopyError` until you `tether new` again. This is jj's
stale-working-copy check applied to external branches.

## Drift

Snapshots happen on every command, so drift is caught at the next touch rather
than by a daemon. An Observed object registered as immutable (the default for
`file`) that changes on disk is an *error* at `status`; a Forkable object whose
working branch moved is simply `modified` and will be pinned on the next
commit. `verify` answers the other question -- do the pins we recorded still
resolve to the states we recorded? -- cheaply by default, deeply with `--deep`,
and across every commit with `--all-history`.

## Listings

A directory or prefix state is only a digest, so it cannot be diffed on its
own. At commit time the `file` backend hands tether a per-file listing, stored
content-addressed under `.tether/listings/` and committed with the manifests
(the same trick as DVC's `.dir` files). `diff --content` compares two listings
file by file; `gc` prunes listings no manifest references.

## What tether does not do

- Cross-system atomicity. A commit records each object's state within a
  capture window; point-consistency requires quiesced writers.
- Reimplement history, undo, branching, or sharing. That is the VCS's job.
- Queries or transactions across systems.
